lead: Monitoring gives evidence: logs, metrics and traces record what happened. Auditing proves a control worked by comparing that evidence with policy. Incident response uses both to limit damage in a repeatable loop: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, then learn. Every cloud deployment needs this loop. A UPI payment gateway in Chennai watches failed transactions, a booking site watches a ticket-release spike, and a regulator asks for the audit trail months later. The same evidence supports an SLA claim and a forensic investigation.
prereq: You need: 6.1 threats, 6.2 non-repudiation and 6.5 IAM.

blocks.text: Monitoring rests on three signals. A log is a timestamped record of one event: who called an API, which login failed, which firewall rule dropped a packet. A metric is a number sampled over time: CPU percent, requests per second, error count. A trace follows one request across services and shows where the time went. The three answer what happened, how much, and where.

Cloud providers keep audit trails. An audit trail records control-plane actions: create a bucket, change an IAM role, delete a key. Each entry has a principal, an action, a resource, a time and a result. For non-repudiation the trail must be append-only and read-restricted; see 6.2. The provider logs its control plane. The customer logs the guest OS, the application, data-plane access and the identity provider. Collect both.

An audit picks one control, for example only admins can delete buckets. It tests the control against the audit trail for a chosen period, samples entries, and records pass or fail with the evidence used. The record names the control, the period, the sample and the result.

Every log line carries a timestamp. Clocks drift, so all sources sync to one time service (NTP). Without sync, two events minutes apart can appear reversed, and an attacker can hide a sequence. Set retention before you need it: a 7-day window cannot prove a breach that began a month ago. Logs also hold personal data, so redact and restrict them under your retention policy (see 6.4).

A SIEM (security information and event management) system collects logs from many sources, normalises them, correlates rules, and raises alerts. Example rule: five failed logins from one IP in one minute, then a success. Correlation across sources is the point. A single log line is weak evidence.

Two clocks matter. MTTD (mean time to detect) is the average delay from incident start to alert. MTTR (mean time to recover) is the average delay from incident start to restored service. The two measure different things: MTTD stops at the alert, MTTR runs to restored service. A fast alert alone does not shorten repair, but because MTTR is counted from incident start, faster detection usually does cut downtime.
MTTD = (1/N) Σᵢ (t_alert,i − t_start,i); MTTR = (1/N) Σᵢ (t_recover,i − t_start,i)
blocks.where: N is the number of incidents; t_alert,i is the alert time for incident i; t_start,i is its start time; t_recover,i is its restored-service time; all times use the same unit, usually minutes.

blocks.text: An alert triggers a runbook: a short, tested procedure that says who to call, what to capture and what to disable. Automation can quarantine a VM or revoke a token. Keep a human approval for destructive steps. False positives waste time, so tune rules against a baseline of normal behaviour.

Incident response follows six phases. Some syllabi use six phases (prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn); the NIST guide groups the same steps into four, with containment, eradication and recovery as one phase. Prepare: roles, contacts, runbooks, backups. Detect: alert triage and scope. Contain: isolate the instance, disable the credential, block the IP. Eradicate: patch, rebuild, rotate keys. Recover: restore service and verify integrity. Learn: write the post-incident review and fix the gap.

Preserve evidence before you destroy it. Volatile evidence (memory, running processes, network connections) disappears on reboot. Take a disk snapshot, compute a cryptographic hash, and record who handled it and when. That record is the chain of custody. Do not delete the instance to 'clean up' before the snapshot is verified.

Provider and customer duties split. The provider investigates its platform and supplies audit logs. The customer investigates its own identities, configurations and data. SLA reports come after the fact: uptime, response time and notification time. A provider can meet 99.9% monthly uptime measured across all regions, or over a year, and still have a 3-hour outage in your region. Read the SLA's measurement point and period before you accept the dashboard number.

figure.caption: Detection ends at 10 min and containment at 30 min, so the containment phase lasts only 20 min, yet the service stays down for a full 180 min until recovery.

spec.aria: An incident timeline in minutes: detect from 0 to 10, contain from 10 to 30, eradicate from 30 to 90 and recover from 90 to 180, with a second bar showing total downtime of 180 minutes from start to recovery.

examples.question: An incident starts at 09:00. An alert fires at 09:10, the incident is contained at 09:30, and service is recovered at 12:00. Use the response timeline in the figure (detect 0–10 min, contain 10–30 min, eradicate 30–90 min, recover 90–180 min). Find detection time, time to containment, containment phase duration and total downtime in minutes and hours.
steps: Detection time = alert time − incident start = 09:10 − 09:00 = 10 min.
Time to containment = contained time − incident start = 09:30 − 09:00 = 30 min. Containment phase duration from the figure = 30 min − 10 min = 20 min.
Total downtime = recovered time − incident start = 12:00 − 09:00 = 3 h = 180 min.
Eradication window from the figure = 90 min − 30 min = 60 min; recovery window = 180 min − 90 min = 90 min.
examples.answer: Detection = 10 min, time to containment = 30 min, downtime = 180 min = 3 h; containment phase lasts 20 min, eradication takes 60 min and recovery 90 min.

detect = alert-start
contain = contained-start

contain_phase = 30-10
eradicate = 90-30

traps: Unsynchronised clocks make log correlation unreliable: two events can appear in the wrong order, so an attack sequence looks innocent.
MTTD is not MTTR. MTTD measures start-to-alert delay; MTTR measures start-to-recovery delay. Containment is not recovery.
Provider audit logs cover the control plane. Guest OS logs, application logs and data-plane access are the customer's responsibility.
Rebooting a compromised VM or deleting the instance destroys volatile evidence; snapshot and hash first, then eradicate.
Short log retention defeats auditing. A breach discovered after the retention window leaves no usable trail.

quiz.q: Define log, metric and trace in one line each.
quiz.a: A log is a timestamped event record. A metric is a number sampled over time. A trace follows one request across services.

quiz.q: Why must all log sources use a synchronized clock? Give one failure that clock skew hides.
quiz.a: Without a common time base, events cannot be ordered or correlated. Clock skew can hide a failed-login burst followed by a success by placing the success before the failures.

quiz.q: An incident starts at 02:00, alert at 02:05, contained at 02:20, recovered at 04:00. Find detection time, containment time and downtime in minutes.
quiz.a: Detection = 02:05 − 02:00 = 5 min. Containment = 02:20 − 02:00 = 20 min. Downtime = 04:00 − 02:00 = 2 h = 120 min.

quiz.q: The provider reports 99.95% monthly uptime, but your users saw 3 hours of failure. Explain how both can be true using measurement points and shared responsibility.
quiz.a: The provider measures its own platform endpoints over the month; 99.95% of about 720 h allows about 22 min. Your 3 h failure can come from your configuration, identity provider, DNS or network path, which the provider does not measure. Both statements use different boundaries and measurement points.

quiz.q: List the six incident response phases in order and state the goal of containment.
quiz.a: Prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Containment stops the incident from spreading and limits damage while preserving evidence.

quiz.q: Why should you snapshot and hash a disk before eradicating malware from a VM?
quiz.a: Eradication changes or deletes evidence. A snapshot preserves the disk state; the hash proves the snapshot was not altered, supporting chain of custody for investigation or legal use.

quiz.q: What does SIEM stand for and what does it do?
quiz.a: Security information and event management. It collects and normalises logs, correlates events across sources and raises alerts.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern observability uses OpenTelemetry for vendor-neutral traces, eBPF for kernel-level telemetry without agents, and SOAR platforms to automate runbook steps. Cloud forensics adds legal hold, cross-region log export and immutable buckets. Research looks at tamper-evident logs using hash chains and trusted execution environments. Search terms: OpenTelemetry, eBPF observability, SOAR, cloud forensics chain of custody, tamper-evident logging.
